stories.headline: Tech stocks slide into a week set by Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's IPO
stories.summary: A selloff in technology shares carried into Monday, with U.S. stock futures and emerging-market stocks falling as investors waited on two events: Nvidia's quarterly results on Tuesday and the pricing of Anthropic's initial public offering, expected Wednesday with trading to start Thursday. Weakness in Asian AI stocks overnight added to the pressure, according to The Wall Street Journal.
stories.why_it_matters: A handful of AI companies now make up a large share of the stock indexes held in most 401(k)s and index funds, so how this week goes for Nvidia and Anthropic can move ordinary retirement balances.
stories.background: Since 2023, investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence has driven much of the stock market's gains, led by chipmaker Nvidia, the world's most valuable company by market value. Nvidia's shares have fallen sharply in recent weeks amid a leadership crisis tied to questions about chip sales reaching China. At the same time, Anthropic, the AI lab that makes the Claude models, is preparing one of the largest stock offerings on record. The Nasdaq Composite ended last week down nearly 6% over the past month, while the Dow, which is less tech-heavy, was up over the same period.

facts.text: U.S. stock futures for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell early Monday ahead of Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's market debut.

Bloomberg said the tech selloff carried into a new week as traders avoided risky bets, and that emerging-market stocks fell the most in more than a week as a rout in Nvidia shares weighed on the global AI trade.
Nvidia is scheduled to report earnings on Tuesday.
Anthropic's IPO is expected to price on Wednesday and begin trading Thursday, according to Bloomberg.
Earlier reporting said Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $80 a share and lined up about $26 billion from Nvidia, Google and other companies.
The WSJ reported that venture-capital firms, large tech companies and sovereign-wealth funds that invested early in Anthropic stand to gain heavily from the offering.
The dollar index (DXY) rose to a 19-month high of 103.533, the WSJ reported.

disputed.topic: Whether the AI-driven market is headed for a deep fall

positions.claim: Former White House economist Jason Furman told MarketWatch that if AI proves to be a bubble that bursts, the most likely outcome is about a 25% drop in the broad market.
Morgan Stanley strategists told clients to raise their stock allocation to the maximum, one of the most bullish year-ahead outlooks so far, MarketWatch reported.

Puts Nvidia's 'leadership crisis' next to a 'mega-IPO' in the same line.
Takes the opposite angle: argues Nvidia can avoid the slump of past market-cap leaders.

stories.headline: Bessent says Nvidia should pick an outside CEO after Huang's exit
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' and should look outside the company for its next chief executive, following Jensen Huang's resignation. The New York Post reported that Nvidia also owes the administration answers within 10 days on whether it profited from banned chip sales.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is the largest company in the stock market and its chips power most AI systems, so a leadership fight involving the government affects both retirement funds and U.S.-China tech policy.
stories.background: Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang in 1993, makes the chips used to train most AI systems. The U.S. bars sales of its most advanced chips to China. Earlier this month the company's board opened an investigation into Huang's ties to a former executive of Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, amid reports that U.S. officials suspected her of links to Chinese intelligence. The matter also exposed a rift in the administration: Axios reported that Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over why Megaspeed had not been put on a trade blacklist.

facts.text: Bessent said Nvidia must 'go outside the company' to find a new CEO and called for a 'dramatic shakeup.'
The New York Post described Bessent's remarks as coming after Jensen Huang's resignation.
The Post reported that Nvidia owes the administration answers within 10 days about whether it profited from banned chip sales.
CNBC said Bessent has criticized Lutnick's Commerce Department over suspected chip diversion to China while defending President Trump's handling of the matter.
Axios reported on Nov. 11 that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room over inaction on China; a Lutnick spokesperson denied the exchange took place.
Nvidia's board opened an investigation into Huang's ties to a former Megaspeed executive, and Huang acknowledged a personal relationship with her, according to earlier reports.
The Washington Post reported that Trump's stake in Nvidia grew to as much as $62 million before the scandal broke.

framing.note: Sticks to Bessent's quote about going outside the company.
Names Huang's resignation and the $4 trillion valuation, and adds the 10-day deadline.
Ties the shakeup call directly to a 'China chip scandal.'

coverage.takeaway: Headline only: Bessent's call for an outside CEO.

stories.headline: Treasury yields ease, but a December Fed rate hike stays in view
stories.summary: U.S. Treasury yields dipped Monday after jumping last week on hotter inflation data and hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials, the WSJ reported. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said last week he would back at least a quarter-point rate increase in December and that a half-point move may be needed if core inflation came in hot.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher Fed rates and bond yields feed into mortgage, car-loan and credit-card rates; the 30-year mortgage rate is already above 7%.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve raises its benchmark rate to cool inflation and lowers it to support jobs. Inflation picked up this fall as the war with Iran pushed energy prices higher; consumer prices were up 3.7% from a year earlier in September. The Fed's key rate stands at about 3.9%, while the 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.1% as of Nov. 12. Its next meeting is in December, and markets are now debating the size of a hike rather than whether one comes.

facts.text: Treasury yields fell on Monday following large increases last week that were prompted by inflation data and hawkish Fed comments, the WSJ reported.
Waller said he plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December.
Waller said a half-point hike may be needed if core consumer prices came in hot.
The 2-year Treasury yield had its biggest one-day jump in 19 months on Nov. 10.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only (paywalled): yields dip while hike prospects stay in focus.

stories.headline: Japan's economy unexpectedly shrinks as energy costs bite
stories.summary: Japan's economy contracted at an annualized 0.1% in July-September, its first contraction in a year, according to official data reported by Reuters and the Financial Times. Outlets tied the drop to weak consumer spending under high energy prices, and the FT said it complicates the Bank of Japan's interest-rate plans.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan is the world's fourth-largest economy and a major U.S. trading partner; its slowdown is another sign of how the oil shock from the Iran war is weighing on households worldwide.
stories.background: Japan imports nearly all its oil, so the jump in energy prices since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has hit its households hard. The government had subsidized household energy bills, but those subsidies reportedly ended in September. The Bank of Japan has been slowly raising interest rates after decades near zero, and weak growth makes further increases harder to justify. On Monday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told a government panel that wage growth is 'quite strong.'

facts.text: Japan's GDP shrank at an annualized 0.1% in the July-September quarter.
The contraction was unexpected and the first in a year.
Reuters said inflation was squeezing households; the FT cited weak consumer spending and record-breaking rains.
CNBC said energy subsidies for households had reportedly expired in September, exposing the economy to higher energy prices from the Iran war.
BOJ Governor Ueda told a government panel that wage growth was 'quite strong.'

framing.note: Calls the contraction slight and points to oil prices.

coverage.takeaway: Headline only: gives the annualized 0.1% figure.

stories.headline: Diesel drops below $6 a gallon, easing a key inflation pressure
stories.summary: U.S. retail diesel prices fell below $6 a gallon for the first time since early September, Bloomberg reported, a two-month low driven by easing geopolitical tensions and weaker demand. Goldman Sachs separately forecast a 'sizable' oil surplus next year that it expects to pull prices lower.
stories.why_it_matters: Diesel moves the trucks and farm equipment behind most goods, so cheaper diesel can eventually ease food and shipping costs that have pushed prices up this fall.
stories.background: Diesel prices surged this year as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran disrupted oil supplies and Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries cut fuel output. Because diesel feeds into transport and farming costs, its price has helped push up food and energy inflation. Brent crude, the global benchmark, was around $92 a barrel last week, down about 29% over a month.

facts.text: Retail diesel fell below $6 a gallon for the first time since early September.
The New York Post attributed the decline to easing tensions and weaker demand.
Diesel had surged after the war with Iran disrupted oil supplies and Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries curbed production.
Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel next year and ease to $78 by the end of 2027, citing a sizable supply surplus.

framing.note: Highlights the two-month low and its causes.
